success_factors: Shallow wet ash sealed organic materials; chance discovery during bulldozing; Mesoamerican Pompeii — preserved daily life including plant remains and painted gourds
notes: UNESCO World Heritage. Discovery 1976 during construction of grain silos. 14 structures excavated. Extraordinary organic preservation due to moist tephra. Budget figure estimated from multi-decade NSF-funded excavation.

key_reference: Doumas 1983; Marinatos 1968; Friedrich 2009; Manning et al. 2006
success_factors: Deep pumice sealed multi-story buildings; systematic Greek excavation since 1967; local knowledge of ruins in quarry; good organic preservation under pumice
notes: Discovery 1867 during Suez Canal pumice quarrying. Marinatos began systematic excavation 1967. Upper floors preserved. Frescoes sealed by pumice. No human remains (population evacuated). 2-6m pumice layer, up to 40m total volcanic deposits.

success_factors: Systematic Italian state excavation since 1748; 4-6m pumice/ash sealed intact city; prior literary accounts (Pliny the Younger) guided search; tourism revenue funds ongoing work
notes: 66 hectares total, ~45 hectares excavated. ~1150 human casts. Killed by surge/heat, not ash fall. Ongoing excavation and conservation. Most excavated ancient city.

success_factors: Deeper burial preserved organic materials (wood/papyrus/food); pyroclastic flow sealed rather than collapsed buildings; boathouses contained 300+ skeletons proving no successful evacuation
notes: ~5 hectares excavated of ~20 total. Buried 15-25m by pyroclastic flows. Harder to excavate than Pompeii due to depth and hardened tuff. Modern Ercolano built directly on top.

success_factors: Circular pyramid tip protruded above ~8m Pedregal lava flow; ceremonial center of 20000+ people; lava flow rather than tephra — harder to excavate but excellent preservation below
notes: Covered by Pedregal lava field. Lava 6-10m thick. Date debated — Siebe (2000) argues ~245 CE based on radiocarbon, earlier estimates placed it 100 BCE-600 CE. One of earliest urban centers in Valley of Mexico.

success_factors: Tephra layers provided stratigraphic markers for agricultural phases; swamp environment preserved botanical evidence; drainage project exposed stratigraphy; UNESCO World Heritage
notes: Evidence for independent invention of agriculture ~7000 BP. Multiple tephra layers from Highland eruptions provide chronological markers. Tephra here is BENEFICIAL — aids dating rather than destroying evidence.

estimated_cost_usd: ~250000 for initial LiDAR survey (per campaign, actual)
key_reference: Evans et al. 2013 PNAS; Evans 2016; Pottier 1999
success_factors: LiDAR penetrated dense tropical canopy revealing urban grid extending 35+ km; prior aerial photography (Pottier) identified some features; large-scale systematic survey; included as non-volcanic comparandum for remote sensing method
notes: Not volcanic burial — included as methodological comparandum. LiDAR revealed settlement 10-50x larger than expected. Cost figure from KALC (Khmer Archaeology LiDAR Consortium) 2012 campaign. Directly relevant to tropical survey methodology.

key_reference: Dull et al. 2019; Sheets 1979; Pedrazzi et al. 2019
success_factors: Massive regional tephra blanket; geological mapping identified deposit extent first; archaeological investigation followed; TBJ found across >100 km radius; linked to Maya Hiatus and population displacement
notes: Tierra Blanca Joven (TBJ) eruption devastated western El Salvador. 0.5m tephra at 70 km distance. VEI debated (5-6). Sheets (1979) linked to regional population displacement. Distinct from Ceren (different eruption, 160 years earlier).

key_reference: Voight 1990; Pierson et al. 1990; Naranjo et al. 1986
success_factors: Modern event with full documentation; lahar traveled 60+ km and buried town to 2-5m; 23000 deaths; case study in volcanic hazard response failure
notes: Not archaeological in traditional sense — modern town destroyed. Included because lahar burial mechanism is identical to what E083 documents for Kelud 1919. Demonstrates how quickly settlements disappear under lahars.

success_factors: Pre-eruption archaeological baseline existed (USFS surveys); tephra stratigraphy from multiple historic eruptions; controlled modern experiment in volcanic burial; Forest Service systematic survey
notes: Multiple pre-1980 eruptions left tephra layers useful for dating (set Y ~3500 BP, set P ~2500 BP, etc.). 1980 tephra reached 0.15-1m locally. Pre-eruption surveys meant baseline existed for comparison — rare controlled scenario.

key_reference: Wilson & Walker 1985; Lowe et al. 2008; Holdaway & Beavan 1999; Hogg et al. 2012
success_factors: Massive eruption predates Polynesian settlement (~1250 CE) so direct burial of sites unlikely; BUT Taupo tephra is critical chronostratigraphic marker across New Zealand; Maori oral traditions record volcanic activity
notes: Important clarification: Taupo ~232 CE eruption PREDATES Maori settlement by ~1000 years. No Maori sites were buried. However Taupo Pumice is a key stratigraphic marker for ALL NZ archaeology. Included for methodological importance, not as burial case.

key_reference: Oppenheimer 2003; Sigurdsson & Carey 2015; Gao et al. 2006
success_factors: 2004 excavation by Sigurdsson found Sumbawan village buried under 3m pyroclastic flow; carbonized house + occupants (Pompeii of the East); oral traditions guided search; prior geological mapping of deposits
notes: Kingdom of Tambora (~10000 people) obliterated. Sigurdsson began archaeological excavation 2004 near Pancasila village. Found carbonized house with 2 occupants, bronze bowls, pottery. Buried under ~3m pyroclastic flow. Very limited excavation to date.

success_factors: Chance discovery by farmer; shallow plowing hit stone blocks; government excavation revealed complete Hindu temple buried 6.5m; demonstrates ongoing Merapi sedimentation burying Mataram-era sites
notes: Discovered 1966 when farmer's plow struck stone. Complete Shiva temple with linga-yoni. 6.5m burial depth. Excavated by Suaka Peninggalan Sejarah dan Purbakala. Near Yogyakarta airport. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-014.

success_factors: Sand miners discovered stone structures at 5-7m depth; government rescue excavation; Hindu temple complex partially excavated; demonstrates same burial process as Sambisari 27 years later — ongoing Merapi sedimentation
notes: Discovered 1993 during commercial sand mining (ironic: volcanic sand mining uncovered volcanically-buried temple). Burial depth 5-7m. Only partially excavated. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-015.

success_factors: Largest Buddhist monument; partially buried by volcanic ash and jungle; Raffles ordered clearing 1814; Dutch restoration 1907-1911; UNESCO mega-restoration 1975-1982
notes: Not fully buried like Sambisari — upper terraces remained visible but lower galleries and base buried. Volcanic sedimentation + tropical vegetation. Restoration cost $25M (UNESCO Borobudur project). Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-013.

success_factors: Colonial reports documented 1-4.28m burial of Majapahit structures; continued Indonesian excavation; site extends ~100 km2 but most structures buried; local brick mining has been both destructive and revelatory
notes: Majapahit capital (~1293-1500 CE). Colonial-era Dutch surveys found walls, foundations, statues at 0.75-4.28m depth (multiple OV reports). Arjuno-Welirang lahar/sedimentation responsible. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-030 through TAC-037.

success_factors: Bathing pool/petirtaan of Majapahit court buried 3.5m; chance discovery; complete Majapahit royal bathing complex; demonstrates that even monumental architecture becomes invisible at 3+ m burial
notes: Part of Trowulan/Majapahit complex. Royal bathing complex (petirtaan). Buried 3.5m under volcanic sediment. Name means 'rat temple' — rats were first to find it. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-035.

success_factors: Known temple complex but 4th row temples completely underground; Vishnu statue found at 9.14m depth during well digging; demonstrates that even at famous sites there are deeply buried unknown structures
notes: Main temples restored, but 4th row temples remain underground (OV 1920). Silver Vishnu statue found 9.14m deep near Prambanan (OV 1925) — deepest documented burial in E083 dataset. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-011, TAC-018.

success_factors: Highland plateau temples partially buried and waterlogged; burial mound at 2.5m depth; ongoing volcanic gas emissions complicate archaeology; temples originally much more numerous
notes: Dieng temples (~8th-9th c.) on active volcanic plateau. OV 1912 reports 2.5m burial depth for one mound. Volcanic gases (CO2, H2S) killed 149 people in 1979 — active hazard. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-043, TAC-044.

success_factors: Group of 9 Hindu temples on Ungaran slopes; partial burial and collapse due to volcanic/slope processes; only 3.5 km from Ungaran summit; demonstrates that even documented sites suffer ongoing volcanic destruction
notes: Name means 'nine buildings' — originally more structures. At 3.5 km from Ungaran summit. Ongoing collapse and burial. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-045.

success_factors: Colonial surveyors documented temple damage/burial immediately after 1919 lahar; Candi Ponggoh and Sumber Nanas buried ~2m; Panataran narrowly missed; demonstrates stochastic nature of volcanic destruction
notes: 7 sites affected in single eruption event: 2 buried, 1 destroyed (statues swept away), 4 near-misses. Colonial OV reports provide contemporary primary documentation. Key VOLCARCH evidence — E083 TAC-003 through TAC-009.

key_reference: Druitt et al. 1999; Fytikas et al. 1990
success_factors: Post-Minoan volcanic activity on Santorini including Nea Kameni island formation; multiple small eruptions documented historically; relevant for understanding multi-phase volcanic impact on same region
notes: Santorini has had 12+ eruptions since the Minoan event. Nea Kameni (formed 46 CE-1950 CE) is built entirely of post-Minoan lava. Historical harbor blocked repeatedly. Not direct archaeological burial but demonstrates continuous volcanic hazard at inhabited sites.

key_reference: De Caro & Guzzo 1979; Clarke 2003; Thomas & Clarke 2007
success_factors: Luxury Roman villa (Villa A of Poppaea) preserved under same tephra as Pompeii; extraordinary frescoes; Villa B commercial — 54 human remains with jewelry/coins suggesting attempted flight; systematic Italian excavation
notes: Two villas (A and B) buried by Vesuvius 79 CE. Same event as Pompeii/Herculaneum. Villa A attributed to Nero's wife Poppaea. UNESCO World Heritage (part of Pompeii designation). Less visited than Pompeii but equally well preserved.

key_reference: Miniero 2003; Parslow 1995; Restoring Ancient Stabiae Foundation
success_factors: Multiple luxury villas preserved under Vesuvius 79 CE tephra; Pliny the Elder died here; Bourbon excavation → backfilled → re-excavated modern era; RAS Foundation (international collaboration) model for site management
notes: Ancient resort town. Pliny the Elder died at Stabiae during 79 CE eruption. Multiple villas with frescoes (Villa San Marco, Villa Arianna). Excavated 1749-1782 then backfilled; re-excavation since 1950s. Less known than Pompeii but large site.

success_factors: Pre-Hispanic settlements repeatedly affected by Popocatepetl eruptions; tephra layers provide chronological markers; population displacement documented archaeologically; demonstrates cyclical abandonment-reoccupation pattern
notes: Multiple eruptions affected Puebla-Tlaxcala valley. Plunket & Uruñuela documented abandonment episodes. Tetimpa site buried under ~2m Popocatepetl tephra. Archaeological evidence for abandonment → reoccupation cycles.

success_factors: Not volcanic burial — included as volcanic landscape comparandum; settlement used volcanic obsidian; famous mural may depict eruption of Hasan Dagi; demonstrates volcanic awareness in Neolithic communities
notes: NOT buried by volcanic deposit. Included because: (1) famous wall painting possibly depicting Hasan Dagi eruption ~6600 BCE (Schmid et al. 2019 confirmed), (2) volcanic obsidian economy, (3) demonstrates ancient volcanic awareness — relevant to P11 volcanic informedness thesis.

key_reference: Newhall & Punongbayan 1996; Rodolfo et al. 1996; Gaillard 2007
success_factors: Modern event with full scientific documentation; secondary lahars continued burying lowlands for years after eruption; Aeta indigenous communities displaced; demonstrates that lahar burial is a PROCESS not an event — ongoing for 5+ years post-eruption
notes: 1991 eruption deposited 5-6 km3 of tephra. Secondary lahars redeposited material for years, burying towns and agricultural land under 1-10m. ~200 deaths from eruption, ~300+ from lahars 1991-1997. Directly analogous to Kelud/Merapi lahar processes in Java.

key_reference: Cioni et al. 1999; Mastrolorenzo et al. 2006; Sevink et al. 2011
success_factors: Bronze Age settlements buried by Avellino eruption ~3900 BP; footprints preserved in wet ash (Mastrolorenzo et al. 2006); demonstrates that Vesuvius had major pre-79 CE impacts; multiple burial cycles at same volcano
notes: Avellino pumice eruption (~1995 BCE) buried Bronze Age settlements NW of Vesuvius. Human footprints preserved in pyroclastic surge deposit near Avellino. Shows 79 CE was not Vesuvius's first catastrophic impact on human settlement.
